To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

forest cover expansion in the Panama Bayano-Darién agricultural frontier is simultaneous to and subsequent of a preceding pattern land-use/cover changes characterized by expanding ranchlands and depopulation.
forest cover expansion in the Bayano-Darian agricultural frontier of Panama is simultaneously to and successive of preceding deforestation.

the forest-transition theory is not applicable to all forest transitions, that forest transitions are not always preceded by deforestation, and that forest transitions can be preceded by a variety of land-use/land-cover change processes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the dynamics of forest cover change are affected by land-use/cover changes that precede them, in terms of the spatial and temporal patterns of the forest transition.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
forest transition theory has been proven wrong.
forest transitions are not always a function of a forest transition.
the forest transition is not a universal phenomenon, but a regional one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the forest-transition theory of reforestation is best applied to the study of forest regeneration after deforestation, rather than to the study of reforestation amidst deforested landscapes.
the forest transition theory is a theory of forest regeneration that is not necessarily a theory of forest transition.
forest transitions may occur amidst deforestation and that the nature, drivers and limitations of a forest transition may be determined by antecedent land-use/cover patterns.
The main takeaway from our work is that
forest transitions are not necessarily the product of a single, universal process of forest cover expansion.
the forest transition is not an inevitable process of reforestation, but rather a contingent process whose likelihood is influenced by antecedent deforestation.
forest transition research should be more attentive to the historical land-use context and the antecedent pathways that precede the transition.
